p.title: Negative Link Prediction in Social Media

ext.title: Negative Link Prediction in Social Media
ext.coverage: Read the full extracted text (1,523 lines, pages 87-96, abstract through references). Metadata hint confirmed: title, authors, WSDM 2015 and DOI match the text. No lobbying, elections, legislators, persuasion/turnout or text-measurement content appears in this paper. Figure 4 (cross-site generalization) and Figures 2, 3 and 5 are axis labels only in the extraction, so plotted values are not recoverable; only numbers stated in prose or tables are reported. No Paul markup files were supplied (the task listed none), so paul_markup is empty.
ext.research_question: Can negative (distrust/foe) links be predicted in social media when no negative links are observed, using only positive links and content-centric user interactions (likes/dislikes, ratings, posted opinions)? (Abstract; Sec. 1; Sec. 2, Eq. 1: f: {Gp, A, O} -> Gn.)
ext.theory: Balance theory (Heider; Cartwright and Harary) and status theory (Leskovec et al.) as structural constraints on signed triads, plus the empirical claim that negative interactions (disagreement/antagonism) correlate with negative links. The "enemies are close" pattern (negative-link pairs sit within a few hops in the positive network) motivates the features (Sec. 3.1-3.3).
ext.data: Two sites with explicit trust/distrust or friend/foe links, used for analysis and ground truth. Epinions: 14,765 users, 272,513 positive links, 52,704 negative links, 612,321 posts, 6,937,986 positive opinions, 163,502 negative opinions. Slashdot: 7,275 users, 67,705 positive links, 20,851 negative links, 300,932 posts, 1,742,763 positive opinions, 42,260 negative opinions (Table 1, p. 89). Unit of analysis: ordered user pair. Imbalance of negative to missing pairs is 1:4131 (Epinions) and 1:2534 (Slashdot) (Sec. 4.1, p. 90). Collection period is not stated. Epinions opinions come from helpfulness ratings (>3 positive, <3 negative); Slashdot opinions come from MPQA-lexicon polarity of comments (Sec. 3, p. 88). Users with no positive or negative links were filtered out.
ext.method: Descriptive analysis (shortest-path distributions, balance and status triad counts, a two-sample t-test and ratio curves), then a supervised classifier, NeLP. Labels: missing pairs are positive samples; negative samples come from pairs with negative interactions (Algorithm 1), refined by status-theory removals and additions, with reliability weights W = f(Nij) if Nij > 0, else r, where f(x) = 1 - 1/log(1+x) (Eq. 2; Sec. 4.1, 5.2). Features: 45 per pair (8 user features for each member, 7 pair features, 22 signed features including 16 weighted triads from Leskovec et al.) (Sec. 4.2). Model: soft-margin SVM with separate costs Cp (positives) and Cn (negatives), per-sample negative weights cj, and a balance-theory Laplacian regularizer weighted by Cb (Eqs. 4-6), solved in dual QP form with a kernel (Eqs. 7-15). Parameters: Cp=1, Cn=0.5, Cb=0.1 (Epinions); Cp=1, Cn=0.7, Cb=0.01 (Slashdot) (Sec. 5.2). Baselines: Random; sPath (predict negative for pairs at a fixed shortest-path length); negIn (predict negative for pairs with negative interactions); negInS (negIn refined by status-theory steps); NeLP-negIn (NeLP trained on negIn labels). Parameterized baselines are reported at their best setting (Sec. 5.2, p. 93).
ext.identification_strategy: None in a causal sense. Prediction is framed as supervised classification with constructed (noisy) labels. Evidence for signal comes from a t-test and conditional ratios (Sec. 3.3). Generalization is checked by training on one site and testing on the other (Sec. 5.2, Fig. 4). Ablations remove components (Cn, cj, Cb) one at a time (Sec. 5.3, Tables 4-5) and vary Cb over {0, 0.001, 0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.5, 1} (Sec. 5.4, Fig. 5). The text does not describe the train/test split, folds, or how evaluation negatives were drawn.
ext.scope: Population: online users of two platforms (Epinions product-review trust network; Slashdot technology-news friend/foe network). No institutional or regulatory setting. Era: not stated; the datasets are pre-2015 snapshots. Claims are limited to these two platforms and to pairs with at least one positive link or interaction. Generalization is tested only between these two sites.

key_findings.finding: Negative-link pairs sit close together in the positive network: about 82.64% (Epinions) and 87.86% (Slashdot) are within 3 hops; over 45% have shortest path below 3 and over 80% below 4.
Triads are mostly balanced and satisfy status theory, supporting both theories as structural constraints.

Pairs with negative interactions are much more likely to have a negative link than randomly matched pairs; the t-test rejects H0 at alpha=0.01. The ratio of negative-link pairs rises with the number of negative interactions K.
NeLP is best on both sites. Random and sPath are near zero; negIn is a strong heuristic; negInS and NeLP-negIn improve on it; full NeLP is top on F1 and precision.
Status-theory refinement (negInS over negIn) gives a small relative F1 gain on both sites.
A classifier trained on one site transfers to the other with little loss, so the features are site-general.
key_findings.numbers: Figure values not extractable; text says the decrease is 'remarkably little' in both directions

key_findings.finding: Ablations show each component contributes. Using cj=1 (no interaction-based reliability) cuts precision the most. Removing balance regularization (Cb=0) also hurts.
key_findings.numbers: Epinions full NeLP F1 0.3242 / P 0.2861; Cn=1 gives 0.3188/0.2793; cj=1 gives precision 0.2612 (-8.70%); Cb=0 gives 0.3084/0.2686; all removed gives 0.2992/0.2342. Slashdot full 0.2441/0.2139; cj=1 precision 0.1902 (-11.08%); Cb=0 gives 0.2347/0.1972; all removed gives 0.2213/0.1722

key_findings.finding: Balance regularization is sensitive to Cb. Precision rises from Cb=0 to 0.001, is flat over a middle range, and drops sharply at large Cb.
key_findings.numbers: Precision +4.02% (Epinions) and +4.41% (Slashdot) from Cb 0 to 0.001; stable from 0.001 to 0.1 in Epinions; sharp drop after about 0.05 in Slashdot

key_findings.finding: Accuracy is rejected as a metric because of extreme class imbalance. Precision and F1 are reported on the negative class.
key_findings.numbers: A trivial all-missing classifier can reach 99.99% accuracy in a sparse network (text example)

measures: Negative-class F1-measure (harmonic mean of precision and recall, Sec. 5.1)
Shortest-path length between ui and uj in the positive network (BFS; 'inf' if unreachable)
Share of negative-link pairs within k hops
Triad balance (four sign patterns, two balanced) and status-theory consistency
Pair-level count of negative interactions Nij
Ratio of pairs with negative links among pairs with at least K negative interactions
Two-sample t-test on negative-link indicators for interacting vs matched pairs
Relative F1 and precision change in ablations
Weighted in/out-degree and Jaccard coefficients on positive and negative links, plus 16 weighted triads (45 features total)
limitations: Negative labels are not observed. Training labels are constructed from negative interactions and status-theory refinement, and the paper says they are noisy, especially for negatives (Sec. 4.3, p. 91; Sec. 7, p. 95).
Negative links in Epinions and Slashdot serve only as ground truth for analysis and evaluation; the model itself does not use them (Sec. 3, p. 88).
Opinion labels are proxies: Epinions helpfulness ratings are thresholded at 3, and Slashdot comment polarity comes from the MPQA lexicon (Sec. 3, p. 88).
Severe class imbalance (1:4131 and 1:2534), so precision and F1 stay modest (best F1 0.3242 Epinions, 0.2441 Slashdot) (Sec. 4.1, Table 3).
Balance regularization uses only pairs at shortest-path length 2 plus the labeled sets, a simplification for scale (Sec. 4.3, p. 92).
Parameterized baselines are reported at their best setting, and NeLP parameters differ per site (Sec. 5.2, p. 93). The text gives no held-out tuning protocol.
The evaluation protocol is incomplete: the text does not describe the train/test split, folds, or how evaluation negatives were drawn.
User-generated content (text) is not used, and only one classifier family (soft-margin SVM) is tested (Sec. 7, p. 95).
Only two platforms with explicit signed links are studied. Collection period is not stated, and the datasets are older snapshots, so transfer to current platforms is untested.
Recall is defined (Sec. 5.1) but not reported separately; only precision and F1 appear.

rel.summary_md:
Tang, Chang, Aggarwal and Liu (WSDM 2015) ask whether distrust or foe links can be predicted when none are observed, using only positive links and content interactions. They test this on Epinions (14,765 users, 52,704 negative links) and Slashdot (7,275 users, 20,851 negative links). They report three facts. First, negative-link pairs sit close together in the positive network: 82.64% and 87.86% are within 3 hops. Second, signed triads are mostly balanced (92.31% and 93.01%). Third, pairs with negative interactions are far more likely to hold a negative link (t-test p = 5.72e-89 and 1.93e-109). Their SVM, NeLP, adds reliability weights that grow with the interaction count, plus a balance-theory regularizer. Even so, the best F1 on the negative class is only 0.3242 on Epinions and 0.2441 on Slashdot. The simple rule "a negative interaction means a negative link" (negIn) reaches a precision of only 0.2097 and 0.1483. Precision drops the most (-8.70% and -11.08%) when the count-based reliability weights are removed.

For Paul's systems, the paper's main point is a caution. Melange's signed member-reference layer builds negative edges directly from LLM-scored negative references. That is the paper's negIn signal, which the paper shows to be a real but low-precision proxy for an antagonistic relationship. Congress has no explicit foe declaration, so the system cannot score its reference signs against ground truth the way Tang does. Its negative edges should therefore be read as a measure of negative interaction, not of negative ties. The diagnostic signed-coalition partition uses these signs with no evidence-count floor, while the dashboard drawing does use one. The paper's balance statistics support the sign-product logic in the two-hop stance composer. They also give a cheap test the system could run: are negative-reference dyads close together in the cosponsor graph? Every result here comes from 2015-era online trust platforms, not legislatures.

bearings.paper_claim: Negative interactions predict negative links far above chance (t-test p = 5.72e-89 Epinions, 1.93e-109 Slashdot), but as a classifier the rule 'negative interaction implies negative link' (negIn) reaches only precision 0.2097 / F1 0.2826 on Epinions and 0.1483 / 0.1986 on Slashdot. The share of pairs that hold a negative link rises with the number of negative interactions K, and the paper weights each pair's reliability by f(Nij) = 1 - 1/log(1+Nij).
bearings.paper_location: Sec. 3.3, pp. 89-90, Fig. 3; Sec. 4.1 Eq. 2; Sec. 5.2 Table 3, p. 93
bearings.system_side: The layer counts an LLM-valenced reference as a signed directed edge. The edge's sign and size come from net = (pos - neg) / substantive contexts. One scored negative context therefore gives net = -1.0, the same as ten unanimous negative contexts. The current member_references.json on disk (read 2026-10-09; denominator = 7,944 directed substantive edges, whole cached corpus) has 1,161 edges with net < 0 and 6,028 with net > 0. These counts come from a single path and are UNVERIFIED. The dashboard draws only edges with n_scored >= 2, but the artifact itself keeps single-context edges.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Tang has ground-truth distrust declarations to score interaction-derived signs against. Congress has no equivalent, so the transferable lesson concerns interpretation, not a calibrated precision figure. A negative reference is evidence of a negative interaction, not a validated antagonistic relationship. The paper's interaction signals are thresholded helpfulness ratings and MPQA comment polarity, a weaker reader than an LLM working on a formality-filtered context. Precision here could be higher or lower, and that is untested. The evidence is strongest for the claim that sign evidence becomes more reliable as the count of contexts grows.

bearings.paper_claim: Balance holds in 92.31% (Epinions) and 93.01% (Slashdot) of signed triads, which supports balance as a structural constraint. When signs come from interactions rather than declared links, removing the count-based reliability weights cuts precision by 8.70% and 11.08%, and the balance regularizer helps only at small weight (Cb from 0.001 to 0.1). Large Cb hurts.
bearings.system_side: The Aref-Neal frustration-minimizing partition takes sign(net) and weight |net| from member_references.json. MINW defaults to 0.0, and there is no n_scored floor. A one-context negative reference therefore enters with full weight 1.0 and can frustrate the partition as much as a well-evidenced dyad. The output is a diagnostic that the chain does not consume.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Tang's balance figures come from declared trust/distrust networks among online users. The system's signs are interaction-derived, the paper's noisy-label case. Some of the frustration and of the 'splinter' roster may therefore reflect label noise rather than hidden coalitions. A low-cost check that stays within project rules is a diagnostic sensitivity run with the n_scored >= 2 floor the dashboard already uses. The paper does not show what share of the system's frustration is noise.

bearings.paper_claim: Signed triads in two real signed networks are overwhelmingly balanced: 92.31% (Epinions) and 93.01% (Slashdot). Over 9 in 10 triads obey the sign-product rule (the enemy of my enemy is a friend).
bearings.system_side: compose() sets cu_alignment to the product of stance toward a target and the target's CU valence. Support for a CU-positive target counts as support, and opposition to a CU-negative target also counts as support. This is a balance-theory sign product over a speaker, target, CU triad.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper's triads are person-to-person trust links. The system's third node is an interest (credit unions), reached through a curated valence registry. The paper gives only a structural prior that sign products usually hold. The system's own measurements bound it more tightly: 0.872 with oracle valence and 0.782 with 5-fold CV of the registry, against a 0.677 flat baseline. The bearing is weak, and it does not validate the registry.

bearings.paper_claim: With negative-to-missing imbalance of 1:4131 and 1:2534, accuracy misleads: a trivial classifier can reach 99.99%. The paper therefore reports precision and F1 on the rare class. It also reports parameterized baselines at their best setting and tunes NeLP per site, without a held-out tuning protocol.
bearings.system_side: The forecaster is scored on rare positive joins using AUC, average precision and bill-averaged precision@10/25/50. It is compared against named baselines (B1 member propensity) with average precision as the comparison metric, never accuracy. The forecast is frozen before scoring.
bearings.transfer_conditions: This bears on the choice of metric only, which carries across domains. Tang's best-setting baseline reporting and per-site tuning are what the system's frozen, single-look scoring is built to avoid. The paper is a negative example on protocol, not a template.

gaps_exposed: No evidence-count reliability on signed reference edges. net = (pos-neg)/sub treats a single scored context the same as many unanimous ones, and signed_coalitions.py applies no n_scored floor. Only the dashboard drawing filters at n_scored >= 2.

No ground truth for negative ties. The system cannot estimate the precision of LLM-valenced negative references as relationship indicators. Tang's negIn precision (0.15-0.21) shows that this gap matters.

A cheap untested check: Tang's 'enemies are close' pattern (82.64% and 87.86% of negative pairs within 3 hops of the positive graph) could be measured for negative-reference dyads on the cosponsor graph. The result would show whether negative references sit inside working relationships or across camps.

Signed triad census not reported: the share of balanced triads in member_references.json is not measured. That share would show how much of the Aref-Neal frustration is structural and how much is label noise.

Negative signs never enter the cascade kernel. Out-party sources get a cpf_pressure of 0.5 rather than a negative edge. The paper argues that negative links add value, but this project has not tested that for Congress.
flags: NEAR-REJECTED PROPOSAL: Tang's count-based reliability weight f(Nij) = 1 - 1/log(1+Nij) is a form of per-edge evidence-volume weighting. Per-edge volume normalization was measured and REJECTED in this project. Do not recommend reweighting cascade or SNA edges by volume on this paper's authority. At most, apply the existing n_scored >= 2 floor as a diagnostic sensitivity run on signed_coalitions.

Status theory (94.73% and 93.38% status-consistent triads) concerns directional asymmetry in declared links. It must not be read as evidence for reciprocity, which is NOT validated in this system (D-104..D-108).
The edge counts quoted here (7,944 directed edges, 1,161 with net < 0, as of 2026-10-09 on disk) come from one read path and stay UNVERIFIED until reproduced by a second path (DE-062).
Negative references and signed-partition outputs must not be described as measured hostility, closeness or access (D-025). They are model outputs built on LLM-valenced interactions.
rel.paul_alignment: Paul's position for co-appearance-and-references is that LLM valence per context window answers his question about negative ties. Tang supports this only in part. Negative interactions carry strong signal about negative relationships, but as a direct label they are noisy (negIn precision 0.21 on Epinions and 0.15 on Slashdot), and reliability grows with the number of interactions. The system therefore measures negative interactions, not validated negative ties. Paul's note reads the layer more strongly than this evidence allows, and it does not mention that the diagnostic signed partition uses single-context edges at full weight. For two-hop decomposition, Paul asked how agreement is quantified when two actors share negative sentiment toward a third. Tang's balance census (about 92-93% balanced triads) is direct supporting evidence for the sign-product answer the system already uses in compose(), though from online trust networks rather than Congress. For signed coalitions, the paper supports Paul's interest in Aref-Neal balance partitions but adds the caveat about noisy labels.

related.why: Tang reuses Leskovec et al.'s 16 weighted signed-triad features and signed-link setting, then extends them to the case where no negative links are observed.

Aref and Neal partition a signed House network by generalized balance, the method signed_coalitions.py implements. Tang's balance census and noisy-label results bear on how far that partition can be trusted when signs come from interactions.

This is the same frustration-minimization approach applied to signed political collaboration. Tang supplies the balance-prevalence evidence that motivates it and the caution about interaction-derived signs.
Both are link-prediction papers built on neighbourhood and similarity features. Zareie predicts positive links, and Tang adds the signed and negative-link case.
